source.title: Space to Grow: Unlocking the Final Economic Frontier

chapter.title: The Inflection Point: Crisis into Opportunity

concepts.statement: The shuttle was America's only means of putting humans in space, so its retirement left the US with no homegrown way to reach the ISS and forced it to buy seats on Russia's Soyuz. The authors frame this crisis as the opening that let NASA turn to the commercial sector.
concepts.passage: The shuttle was America's only means of putting humans in space, so its cancellation made apparent to everyone the lack of any homegrown alternatives for launching crew and cargo to the ISS

questions.prompt: When the shuttle retired in 2011, how did the US plan to get its astronauts to the ISS?
questions.answer: Buy seats on Russia's Soyuz rocket
questions.why: With no US vehicle able to carry crew, the only option was paying Russia tens of millions of dollars per seat. The authors call it unthinkable and humiliating for the country that beat the Soviets to the Moon.

distractors.text: Fly them on SpaceX's Dragon capsule
distractors.why: Dragon didn't carry astronauts until 2020, under Commercial Crew. In 2011 it hadn't even delivered cargo to the ISS yet; that came in 2012.

distractors.text: Use Constellation's new crew rocket
distractors.why: Constellation was canceled in 2010, and its crew rocket was never finished.

distractors.text: Keep one shuttle flying until a replacement was ready
distractors.why: After Columbia, the shuttles were set to retire as soon as ISS construction was complete. Atlantis flew the last mission in July 2011.

questions.prompt: The authors call the shuttle's retirement an opportunity as well as a crisis. What was the opportunity?
questions.answer: Room for NASA to turn to the commercial sector
questions.why: The shuttle had dominated NASA's missions and money for thirty years. Its absence, as Bretton Alexander put it, created a void that allowed NASA to look to the commercial sector.

distractors.text: Shuttle money freed up for a return to the Moon
distractors.why: That was Constellation's plan, and it was underfunded, over budget and canceled. The opportunity was a change in how NASA works, not a pot of money.

distractors.text: An end to jobs-program pressure from Congress
distractors.why: That pressure survived. Even after Constellation was canceled, Congress kept funding many of its components.

distractors.text: A case for restoring NASA's Apollo-era budget
distractors.why: NASA's share of federal spending has stayed around 0.5%. The gap changed how NASA works, not how much it gets.

concepts.statement: The early space program was centrally run because its priorities (national prestige, national security, science, exploration) are public goods, which markets underprovide and governments do best.
concepts.passage: the priorities of the early space program—national prestige, national security, science, and exploration—are classic examples of activities that governments do best, what economists call public goods

questions.prompt: According to the authors, why was central government control a natural fit for the early US space program?
questions.answer: Its goals were public goods markets underprovide
questions.why: National prestige, security, science and exploration are classic public goods. Government set the goals; private contractors still built most of the hardware.

distractors.text: Rockets were too risky an investment for private firms
distractors.why: That risk is why NASA used cost-plus contracts, which made firms willing to do the work. It explains how NASA contracted, not why government set the goals.

distractors.text: The Soviet lead left no time for a market to develop
distractors.why: The Soviet lead explains the urgency. The authors' argument is about the kind of goal: markets underprovide prestige, security and science however much time they have.

distractors.text: Congress wanted space jobs spread across key districts
distractors.why: That's the concentrated-interest pressure the authors list as a weakness that grew over time, not the original rationale.

questions.prompt: By the chapter's logic, which space activity is the weakest candidate for handing to the market?
questions.answer: A basic-science probe to the outer planets
questions.why: Basic research is a public good with no paying customer, so a market would underprovide it. The other three are services the chapter shows companies already selling.

distractors.text: Routine cargo delivery to a space station
distractors.why: COTS and CRS showed companies can do this for a fraction of NASA's cost.

distractors.text: Launching commercial communications satellites
distractors.why: SpaceX began doing exactly this on rockets developed under COTS.

distractors.text: Suborbital tourism flights
distractors.why: Blue Origin's New Shepard became the world's leading suborbital tourism vehicle.

concepts.statement: Central control has three structural weaknesses: without competition there are weak incentives for efficiency and innovation; price signals deteriorate, so resources can't be allocated well; and officials face pressure to serve concentrated interests.
concepts.passage: The lack of the competition that you see in a free market means there are limited incentives for efficiency and innovation. Over time, price signals deteriorate, so determining the best way to allocate resources becomes nearly impossible

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the three structural weaknesses of central control the authors identify?
questions.answer: Political swings that disrupt long technical projects
questions.why: Some people blamed politics for mangling yearslong projects, but the authors say it 'wasn't really anyone's fault': the problem was structural. Their three weaknesses are missing competition, deteriorating prices and concentrated interests.

distractors.text: Weak incentives for efficiency without competition
distractors.why: One of the three. Without competitors, there is little push to cut costs or innovate.

distractors.text: Price signals that deteriorate over time
distractors.why: One of the three. Without prices, planners can't tell what things really cost or are worth.

distractors.text: Pressure on officials to serve concentrated interests
distractors.why: One of the three. The shuttle-and-station 'jobs program' is the chapter's example.

questions.prompt: Which problem follows specifically from the loss of price signals under central control?
questions.answer: Planners can't tell where resources do the most good
questions.why: Prices carry information about true costs and benefits. Without them, allocating resources well becomes nearly impossible, however well-meaning the planners.

distractors.text: Contractors pad costs because margins are guaranteed
distractors.why: That's an incentive problem, from cost-plus contracting. Contractors would pad a reimbursed bill even if good prices existed.

distractors.text: Spending gets steered to districts with space jobs
distractors.why: That's the concentrated-interest weakness, a separate one of the three.

distractors.text: Innovation slows because no rival is pushing
distractors.why: That's the competition weakness, a separate one of the three.

concepts.statement: Centralized models perform well against a clear, narrow, fixed goal (Apollo, early Soviet industrialization) and struggle once the task becomes open-ended. The US space program kept its Apollo-era structure after the goal changed.
concepts.passage: America's initial moonshot program of the 1960s had a clear and narrow objective that was well suited to central control. Though the space program accomplished wonders after Apollo, its structure failed to evolve

questions.prompt: What parallel do the authors draw between the Soviet economy and the US space program?
questions.answer: Both did well on fixed goals, badly on open ones
questions.why: The Soviet economy looked invincible while it pursued fixed industrial targets, and Apollo had one clear objective. Both centralized models faltered facing an uncertain frontier. Jim Cantrell's line: the industry that beat the Soviets was 'operating on a Soviet economic model'.

distractors.text: Both lost public support once the space race was won
distractors.why: US public support did fade after Apollo, but that's a point about American opinion, not the parallel the authors draw.

distractors.text: Both bet on one flagship that crowded out every rival
distractors.why: That describes the shuttle's monopoly over US launch, not the Soviet comparison.

distractors.text: Both were run as jobs programs for political allies
distractors.why: Critics called NASA a jobs program. The Soviet parallel is about central planning facing an open-ended frontier.

concepts.statement: From the start, US officials treated space as a national security matter, including the psychological effect of Soviet 'firsts' on national prestige. NASA was created in response to Sputnik (1957) and Gagarin's flight (1961).
concepts.passage: The Soviet Union's success in achieving numerous space "firsts," the document noted, "have resulted in substantial and enduring gains in Soviet prestige," bolstering claims of the Soviet system's "general superiority."

questions.prompt: How did a 1959 US policy statement frame the importance of space?
questions.answer: As national security, including prestige
questions.why: Soviet 'firsts' were seen as substantial and enduring gains in Soviet prestige that bolstered claims of the Soviet system's superiority. The psychological impact counted as a security issue.

distractors.text: As a new frontier for scientific discovery
distractors.why: The statement mentions scientific implications, but frames them all under national security.

distractors.text: As an economic opportunity for American industry
distractors.why: That's the authors' modern lens. In 1959 there was no commercial space market to speak of.

distractors.text: As an arena for cooperation with other nations
distractors.why: That's the ISS's legacy, decades later. In 1959 space was a field of competition with the Soviets.

concepts.statement: NASA's budget peaked in 1966 at 4.4% of federal spending, fell to 1.2% by 1974, and has been around 0.5% for the past decade.
concepts.passage: At its high-water mark in 1966, the agency received $6 billion, or 4.4 percent of the federal budget.

questions.prompt: How did NASA's share of federal spending at its 1966 peak compare with its share today?
questions.answer: Roughly ten times larger
questions.why: 4.4% in 1966 against about 0.5% for the past decade. The 1966 share of today's budget would be about $268 billion.

distractors.text: Roughly twice as large
distractors.why: Far too small. The fall was much steeper.

distractors.text: Roughly four times larger
distractors.why: That's about the drop from 1966 (4.4%) to 1974 (1.2%). It kept falling after that.

distractors.text: Roughly fifty times larger
distractors.why: Too large. Today's share is about 0.5%, not 0.1%.

concepts.statement: Public support for space spending was weak even during Apollo: a year after the Moon landing 56% of Americans said it had not been worth the money. Support fell as the perceived Soviet threat faded.
concepts.passage: one year after the Moon landing (which inspired so many at the time, and so many of today's space leaders), 56 percent felt that it had not been worth the money

questions.prompt: A year after Apollo 11, how did Americans feel about what the Moon landing had cost?
questions.answer: A majority said it hadn't been worth the money
questions.why: 56% said it wasn't worth the money, even though 81% agreed nothing could equal watching it live. Admiration didn't translate into willingness to pay.

distractors.text: Watching it live had made the cost feel worth it
distractors.why: 81% did say nothing could equal watching it live. But 56% still said it hadn't been worth the money.

distractors.text: A majority backed going on to Mars next
distractors.why: Nixon's Space Task Group proposed Mars, stations and a lunar base. The public didn't want to pay for it.

distractors.text: Opinion had swung in favor since 1967
distractors.why: It barely moved: 54% called the program not worth its budget in 1967, and 56% said the landing wasn't worth it in 1970.

questions.prompt: What do the authors connect the post-Apollo fall in support for space funding to?
questions.answer: The fading of the perceived Soviet threat
questions.why: Support for space spending tracked the security rationale. As the Soviet threat from space looked smaller, so did the willingness to pay.

distractors.text: The shuttle's cost overruns
distractors.why: Those came a decade or more later. NASA's budget share had already fallen to 1.2% by 1974.

distractors.text: The Challenger disaster
distractors.why: Challenger was 1986. The decline in support started in the 1960s.

distractors.text: NASA failing to offer a next goal
distractors.why: NASA had an ambitious next plan: stations, a lunar base, a Mars mission. The public didn't want to pay for it.

concepts.statement: NASA's Act One (Apollo) was a rally-the-nation feat, which governments do well. Act Two (shuttle and ISS) required continuous improvement, efficiency and cost reduction, which large government programs do poorly.
concepts.passage: Act Two required the dogged pursuit of continuous improvement, innovation, efficiency, and cost reduction, not typically strengths we associate with large government programs.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental difference the authors draw between NASA's Act One (Apollo) and Act Two (the shuttle and ISS)?
questions.answer: A one-off feat versus steady cost cutting
questions.why: Rallying a nation to pull off a seemingly impossible feat plays to government strengths. Making space access routine and affordable takes steady efficiency gains, which large government programs aren't known for.

distractors.text: Government-run versus commercially run
distractors.why: Act Two was still government-run. The commercial shift came after it, with COTS.

distractors.text: Expendable rockets versus a reusable vehicle
distractors.why: True of the hardware, but the authors' distinction is about the kind of task, not the technology.

distractors.text: Built in-house versus built by contractors
distractors.why: Both acts relied on contractors. About 90% of NASA's space work was contracted out.

questions.prompt: The authors call Operation Warp Speed a modern 'Act One'. Which task would be the closest analogue to an 'Act Two'?
questions.answer: Cutting vaccine production costs year after year
questions.why: Act Two is ongoing, incremental cost and efficiency work, the kind the authors say large government programs struggle with.

distractors.text: Developing a vaccine for a new virus within a year
distractors.why: That's Warp Speed itself: a single urgent feat. Act One.

distractors.text: Building the first working fusion power plant
distractors.why: A single, clearly defined breakthrough. Act One.

distractors.text: Landing the first humans on Mars
distractors.why: The archetypal Act One goal: one feat, one deadline.

concepts.statement: The shuttle's economic case was reusability: a reusable vehicle costs more up front, but if it flies often, the high fixed cost is spread over many launches and the average cost per launch falls.
concepts.passage: if one vehicle could be used over and over, the high initial costs would be worth it because the average cost per launch could fall

questions.prompt: The shuttle cost far more to develop than an expendable rocket. What had to be true for it to be cheaper per launch anyway?
questions.answer: It had to fly often, spreading its fixed costs
questions.why: Reusability pays off only through flight rate. The shuttle was projected to fly sixty missions a year and averaged fewer than five.

distractors.text: It had to come in on its development cost target
distractors.why: It did hit its development target and was still enormously expensive per launch. Operations were the problem.

distractors.text: It had to carry every defense payload
distractors.why: That was how the government tried to raise the flight rate: a means to the condition, not the condition itself.

distractors.text: Its boosters had to be reusable too
distractors.why: More reuse doesn't help if the vehicle rarely flies. Falcon 9 reuses only its first stage and still cut cost per kilogram about twentyfold.

questions.prompt: A startup says its reusable rocket will halve launch prices. Based on the shuttle's history, which question tests that claim most directly?
questions.answer: How many times a year will each vehicle fly?
questions.why: The shuttle's cost case collapsed on flight rate and operating cost, not on development cost or payload.

distractors.text: How much did it cost to develop?
distractors.why: The shuttle hit its development target and still failed on cost.

distractors.text: How much payload can it lift?
distractors.why: The shuttle had a large cargo bay. Capability didn't save its economics.

distractors.text: Is the whole rocket reusable?
distractors.why: Falcon 9 reuses only its first stage and still cut cost per kilogram about twentyfold.

concepts.statement: To give the shuttle enough flights to spread its fixed costs, the government routed all defense payloads to it. This handed it a de facto monopoly, and the existing US private expendable launchers were phased out by the late 1970s.
concepts.passage: The shuttle program was handed a de facto monopoly before it even started, and by the late 1970s US private launch vehicles were phased out.

questions.prompt: In the 1970s the government directed that all defense payloads would fly on the shuttle. What was the main reason?
questions.answer: To spread its fixed costs over more flights
questions.why: A reusable vehicle with high fixed costs pays off only at a high flight rate. Guaranteeing it the defense market was meant to supply that rate, and it also protected Apollo-era NASA and contractor jobs.

distractors.text: Defense had shaped its design and wanted to use it
distractors.why: Defense needs did influence the design, but the payload directive was about the shuttle's economics. Defense later lost enthusiasm for it.

distractors.text: Private rockets had been retired, leaving no alternative
distractors.why: Backwards. Private expendables existed and were flying; they were phased out because the shuttle was given their missions.

distractors.text: Only the shuttle could repair satellites in orbit
distractors.why: A real capability (it famously fixed Hubble), but not why defense payloads were routed to it.

concepts.statement: The shuttle missed its economic goals badly: projected at sixty flights a year, it averaged fewer than five. Development came in on target but operating costs were underestimated by almost two orders of magnitude: about $1.5 billion per launch, roughly $60,000 per kilogram.
concepts.passage: Though NASA hit its development cost target for the shuttles, Scott Pace ... told us that the shuttles' operational costs were underestimated "by almost two orders of magnitude."

questions.prompt: The shuttle was projected to fly sixty missions a year. What did it average over its thirty years?
questions.answer: Fewer than five
questions.why: Less than a tenth of the projection. That shortfall is what wrecked the cost case for reuse.

distractors.text: About fifteen
distractors.why: Too high. Even at its busiest the fleet flew fewer than ten a year.

distractors.text: About thirty
distractors.why: Far too high. It never came close to half the projection.

distractors.text: About forty-five
distractors.why: Far too high. It never came close to the projection.

questions.prompt: Roughly what did it cost the shuttle to put one kilogram of cargo in orbit?
questions.answer: About $60,000
questions.why: About $1.5 billion per launch works out to roughly $60,000 per kilogram in 2008 dollars, nearly $90,000 today.

distractors.text: About $2,800
distractors.why: That's Falcon 9, which the chapter contrasts with the shuttle.

distractors.text: About $6,000
distractors.why: Ten times too low.
Ten times too high.

questions.prompt: The shuttle's cost story has two halves, development and operations. How did each turn out against NASA's estimates?
questions.answer: Development on target; operations vastly underestimated
questions.why: Scott Pace said operating costs were underestimated by almost two orders of magnitude. Building it wasn't the problem; flying it cheaply and often was.

distractors.text: Development far over; operations near target
distractors.why: Reversed. Development came in on target.

distractors.text: Both ran over, with development the larger miss
distractors.why: Development was on target. The miss was almost entirely in operations.

distractors.text: Both were near target; the ISS caused the overrun
distractors.why: The ISS was expensive in its own right, about $100 billion, but each shuttle launch alone cost about $1.5 billion.

concepts.statement: The ISS cost roughly $100 billion to build and $4 billion a year to maintain. Critics said the scientific returns were not commensurate, though the authors credit it as a triumph of diplomacy. The shuttle and ISS together cannibalized NASA's other programs.
concepts.passage: the station cost roughly $100 billion to create and $4 billion a year to maintain, and critics alleged that the scientific returns were "in no way commensurate."

questions.prompt: The authors report sharp criticism of the ISS's cost. What do they credit it with achieving?
questions.answer: A triumph of diplomacy, uniting rivals
questions.why: It brought nations like the US and Russia together on science. Critics said the scientific returns were in no way commensurate with its roughly $100 billion cost.

distractors.text: Making access to orbit routine and affordable
distractors.why: That was the shuttle's goal, and it failed.

distractors.text: Science that justified its price
distractors.why: Critics said the returns were in no way commensurate with the cost.

distractors.text: Returning Americans to deep space
distractors.why: The ISS is in low Earth orbit. Returning to deep space was the goal of Bush's Vision for Space Exploration.

concepts.statement: Pete Worden's 1992 'self-licking ice cream cone' critique: the shuttle and station justified each other (the station could only be built by the shuttle, and the shuttle's main job was building the station), sustaining jobs in key districts and leaving no money to develop anything cheaper.
concepts.passage: the Station is designed so that it can only be built by the Shuttle and the Shuttle is the only way to construct the Station

questions.prompt: What did Pete Worden mean by calling the shuttle and space station a 'self-licking ice cream cone'?
questions.answer: Each program existed mainly to justify the other
questions.why: The station could only be built by the shuttle, and building the station was the shuttle's purpose. The loop absorbed most of NASA's budget and left no money to escape it.

distractors.text: The shuttle cost $1 billion a launch
distractors.why: Worden said that too, but the metaphor is about circular justification, not price.

distractors.text: Both were designed around jobs in key districts
distractors.why: Worden says that's what keeps the loop going. The image itself describes the loop: each program needs the other.

distractors.text: Both delivered spectacle but little science
distractors.why: A criticism made of the ISS, but not what the metaphor means.

questions.prompt: Which situation best fits Worden's 'self-licking ice cream cone'?
questions.answer: A conference held mainly to plan the next one
questions.why: The pattern is circular justification: an activity whose main output is its own continuation.

distractors.text: A supplier that wins only because rivals are barred
distractors.why: That's the shuttle's monopoly pattern: shutting out competition, not justifying itself.

distractors.text: A project whose running costs dwarf its build cost
distractors.why: That's the shuttle's cost pattern.

distractors.text: A program kept alive for the jobs it provides
distractors.why: That's the jobs-program critique. Close, but a program can be propped up by politics without justifying itself in a loop.

concepts.statement: From the Reagan era on, policy endorsed commercial launch (Delta became the first US-licensed commercial vehicle in 1989; the Commercial Space Act passed in 1998), but these efforts stayed marginal because the subsidized, government-run shuttle took the government's missions and most of the funding.
concepts.passage: Government efforts to spark new efficiency and innovation were being squashed by the primacy the government gave to its own vehicles.

questions.prompt: Reagan-era policies endorsed commercial launch, and private rockets were flying by 1989. Why did they stay marginal until the 2000s?
questions.answer: The subsidized shuttle kept the government's business
questions.why: As Wayne Eleazer put it, nothing stopped anyone competing with the shuttle except a heavily subsidized government competitor that would grab 100% of government missions.

distractors.text: Federal law barred companies from competing with NASA
distractors.why: Eleazer's point is the opposite: nothing legally prevented it. The barrier was economic.

distractors.text: Policy let companies launch only commercial satellites
distractors.why: The Reagan measures specifically created pathways for companies to launch government satellites.

distractors.text: No company had yet built a working orbital rocket
distractors.why: McDonnell Douglas's Delta became the first US-licensed commercial vehicle in 1989, and three others soon followed.

concepts.statement: After Columbia, the Aldridge Commission (2004) said NASA must be transformed: buy services from competing private firms instead of owning and operating everything, and limit its own role to what only government can do. Congress wrote this business-first approach into law in 2004.
concepts.passage: NASA's role "must be limited to only those areas where there is irrefutable demonstration that only government can perform the proposed activity."

questions.prompt: The Aldridge Commission in 2004 proposed a test for what NASA should keep doing itself. What was it?
questions.answer: Only what it's demonstrated only government can do
questions.why: NASA's role 'must be limited to only those areas where there is irrefutable demonstration that only government can perform the proposed activity'. It was meant to be restrictive, and Congress wrote the business-first approach into law that year.

distractors.text: Only research and design, leaving manufacturing to industry
distractors.why: Close to the old model: about 90% of the work was already contracted out, with NASA controlling the design. The commission wanted companies designing and owning their vehicles.

distractors.text: Only missions beyond Earth orbit
distractors.why: No geographic line was drawn. The test was a principle about what only government can do.

distractors.text: Only human spaceflight
distractors.why: No mission-type line was drawn. The test was a principle about what only government can do.

questions.prompt: The Aldridge Commission considered recommending that some NASA centers close, then dropped it. Why?
questions.answer: It would have sunk the whole report politically
questions.why: Chairman Edward Aldridge said the report 'would probably have burned on the first day'. A live example of the concentrated-interest pressure the chapter describes.

distractors.text: The centers were needed for Constellation
distractors.why: Constellation came after the report. The obstacle was political.

distractors.text: Its review found the centers ran efficiently
distractors.why: The commission found NASA inefficient and said it needed to be leaner.

distractors.text: NASA's structure was outside its mandate
distractors.why: It explicitly said NASA's organizational structure must be decisively transformed.

concepts.statement: Two approaches to the post-shuttle gap ran in parallel. Constellation was the primary plan: a large, government-owned, Apollo-style program ('Apollo on steroids'), canceled in 2010. COTS was a small ($500 million) commercial program paying companies to develop ISS cargo vehicles. CRS later bought deliveries; Commercial Crew extended the model to astronauts.
concepts.passage: The primary plan was called Constellation, an expansive (and expensive) new program in the Apollo model.

questions.prompt: NASA ran several programs with similar names. Which one paid companies to develop new rockets and cargo vehicles, as opposed to buying deliveries?
questions.answer: COTS
questions.why: COTS funded development of cargo vehicles for the ISS. CRS followed, buying routine deliveries; Commercial Crew extended the model to astronauts.

distractors.text: CRS
distractors.why: The follow-on to COTS. It bought routine cargo deliveries: twelve from SpaceX and eight from Orbital.

distractors.text: Commercial Crew
distractors.why: Extended the COTS model to astronauts, leading to SpaceX's 2020 crew flight.

distractors.text: Constellation
distractors.why: Not commercial at all: a government-owned, Apollo-style program.

questions.prompt: What was the Constellation program?
questions.answer: A government-owned, Apollo-style rocket and lander program
questions.why: NASA Administrator Michael Griffin called it 'Apollo on steroids'. It ran in parallel with COTS, went over budget and behind schedule, and was canceled in 2010.

distractors.text: A follow-on to COTS extending commercial contracts to deep space
distractors.why: Constellation was the government-owned alternative to COTS, not an extension of it.

distractors.text: Bush's 2004 plan to return to the Moon and go on to Mars
distractors.why: That's the Vision for Space Exploration. Constellation was the program built to carry it out.

distractors.text: A program funding companies to build crew vehicles for the ISS
distractors.why: That's Commercial Crew.

concepts.statement: Under traditional FAR contracting, NASA paid contractors cost-plus: their total costs plus a guaranteed profit margin. It existed to insulate companies from the technical and policy risk of ambitious space projects, and about 90% of space program work was contracted this way.
concepts.passage: By guaranteeing that private companies' costs would be covered, plus a margin, FAR made it possible for NASA to contract out much of its equipment needs.

questions.prompt: Under a traditional cost-plus contract, what does the government pay?
questions.answer: All its costs, plus a profit margin
questions.why: Under FAR cost-plus, the government covers total cost and adds an amount for profit. About 90% of space program work was contracted this way.

distractors.text: A set fee for the service, whatever it costs
distractors.why: That's fixed-price, the model COTS switched to.

distractors.text: Fixed payments as each milestone is met
distractors.why: That's how COTS paid. Kistler lost its contract by missing milestones.

distractors.text: Its costs, with no profit on top
distractors.why: Cost-plus adds a guaranteed margin on top of costs. That guarantee is why firms had little reason to cut costs.

questions.prompt: The authors say cost-plus contracting 'was not an accident'. What problem was it designed to solve?
questions.answer: Shielding firms from risky, uncertain projects
questions.why: Space hardware needed huge up-front investment amid technical and policy uncertainty. Guaranteeing costs plus a margin made firms willing to take the work.

distractors.text: Protecting the government from contractor abuse
distractors.why: That was the job of FAR's oversight provisions, layered on top. The cost guarantee itself was about risk.

distractors.text: Ensuring the government owned what it paid for
distractors.why: FAR did give the government the IP, but that wasn't the purpose of reimbursing costs.

distractors.text: Keeping Apollo-era jobs in key districts
distractors.why: Jobs pressure shaped many decisions, but cost-plus was designed to make risky work contractable.

concepts.statement: Criticisms of FAR cost-plus contracting: guaranteed margins gave firms weak incentives to control cost; heavy oversight and documentation burdened new entrants most; and the government took ownership of the technology and intellectual property.
concepts.passage: under FAR contracts, firms had weak incentives to keep costs down and pursue efficiencies, since their margins were guaranteed

questions.prompt: Why did cost-plus contracts give firms weak incentives to keep costs down?
questions.answer: Their margin was guaranteed on any spending
questions.why: If every dollar of cost is reimbursed with a margin on top, spending less earns the firm nothing.

distractors.text: NASA's oversight made design changes slow
distractors.why: Heavy oversight was a real burden, but it's a separate criticism from the incentive problem.

distractors.text: The government owned the technology they built
distractors.why: A real criticism of FAR, but it weakened the incentive to build a wider business, not to cut costs.

distractors.text: NASA dictated the specs
distractors.why: True under FAR, but firms could still cut costs within a spec. With a guaranteed margin they had no reason to.

questions.prompt: Why did FAR contracting weigh hardest on young, small space companies?
questions.answer: They lacked the staff for the paperwork
questions.why: FAR brought heavy requirements, documentation and supervision. Incumbents had the administrative infrastructure to absorb that; new entrants didn't.

distractors.text: Fixed prices exposed them to cost overruns
distractors.why: Reversed. That's the COTS model. Under cost-plus, overruns were reimbursed.

distractors.text: They had to raise private capital to qualify
distractors.why: That's COTS: Kistler lost its contract after failing to raise outside capital.

distractors.text: Its margins were too thin to sustain a startup
distractors.why: The margin was guaranteed on all costs. The burden was administrative.

concepts.statement: COTS used fixed-price contracts: NASA pays a set fee for a service. Financial risk shifts to the company, and the company profits by keeping its costs below the fee, which brings in the efficiency incentives of commercial markets.
concepts.passage: It puts the financial risk on the private companies, but the more that companies can keep their costs below that fee, the more they profit.

questions.prompt: Compared with cost-plus, how does a fixed-price contract handle cost overruns and savings?
questions.answer: The company absorbs overruns and keeps savings
questions.why: With a set fee, every dollar of overrun comes out of the company's pocket and every dollar saved is profit. That's the efficiency incentive COTS brought in.

distractors.text: Government covers overruns; company keeps savings
distractors.why: That would remove the risk and keep the reward. No contract in the chapter works that way.

distractors.text: Overruns and savings are split between them
distractors.why: That's cost-sharing, not fixed-price.

distractors.text: Government covers overruns and recaptures savings
distractors.why: Roughly how cost-plus works: costs are reimbursed, so savings only lower the bill.

concepts.statement: Under COTS, NASA offered 'insight rather than oversight'. Heavy oversight was necessary under cost-plus because firms had an incentive to inflate costs. Fixed-price removed that incentive, so NASA could give companies design freedom while still sharing its expertise.
concepts.passage: oversight was imperative in a cost-plus approach where companies had every incentive to inflate costs

questions.prompt: Heavy oversight was standard under cost-plus. Why was it no longer necessary under COTS?
questions.answer: Fixed prices removed the incentive to inflate costs
questions.why: Oversight was imperative when companies had every incentive to inflate costs. Under a fixed price, padding only hurts the company, so NASA could offer insight (its engineers' expertise) rather than oversight.

distractors.text: Space Act Agreements didn't require it
distractors.why: The agreements made the change legally possible. The reason oversight was no longer needed is the fixed price.

distractors.text: Companies kept their IP
distractors.why: IP retention was about NASA being one customer among many.

distractors.text: Two competing providers kept each other honest
distractors.why: NASA kept two providers as a hedge in case the approach stumbled, not as a substitute for oversight.

concepts.statement: Under COTS, NASA aimed to be 'one customer among many'. The clearest signal was letting companies keep the intellectual property for what they developed, so they could sell the same vehicles to other customers.
concepts.passage: NASA explicitly sought to be just "one customer among many" for its COTS partners, a goal made manifest by its allowing companies to keep the intellectual property rights to their new technologies.

questions.prompt: NASA wanted to be 'one customer among many' for its COTS partners. Which feature do the authors single out as making that goal real?
questions.answer: Letting companies keep their own IP
questions.why: Under the old rules the government took ownership of the technology, so a company had nothing to sell anyone else. Keeping the IP let SpaceX sell Falcon 9 launches to commercial customers.

distractors.text: Paying a fixed price, not reimbursing costs
distractors.why: A key COTS feature, but it's about efficiency incentives, not other customers.

distractors.text: Funding two competing providers
distractors.why: A hedge against failure, not a route to other customers.

distractors.text: Using Space Act Agreements, not FAR
distractors.why: The legal vehicle for COTS, not what made the goal real.

concepts.statement: The first COTS awards (2006) went to SpaceX and Rocketplane Kistler. Kistler failed to raise enough private capital, missed milestones and lost its contract to Orbital Sciences, showing NASA would act as a real customer. SpaceX raised slightly more privately than NASA put in.
concepts.passage: It began missing milestones, and NASA terminated its contract. The agency, it appeared, was taking its new role as a customer seriously.

questions.prompt: Rocketplane Kistler was one of the first two COTS winners and lost its contract. What went wrong?
questions.answer: It couldn't raise enough private capital
questions.why: Kistler couldn't raise enough outside money to fund development, began missing milestones, and NASA terminated the contract. Orbital Sciences took it over. NASA was acting like a real customer.

distractors.text: Its costs overran the fixed price
distractors.why: It was behind schedule, not over a price cap. The root cause was a lack of private capital.

distractors.text: Its rocket failed repeatedly in tests
distractors.why: That was SpaceX, which was blowing up rockets at an alarming rate and still completed all its milestones.

distractors.text: NASA consolidated funding behind SpaceX
distractors.why: NASA gave Kistler's contract to Orbital Sciences, keeping two providers.

questions.prompt: Who paid for most of SpaceX's costs during COTS?
questions.answer: Private investors, a bit more than NASA
questions.why: NASA put in nearly $400 million, slightly less than half. SpaceX raised just over $450 million privately, including $100 million from Musk. Companies were expected to bring their own capital, which is where Kistler failed.

distractors.text: NASA, covering nearly all of it
distractors.why: NASA's share was slightly less than half.

distractors.text: Elon Musk, personally
distractors.why: Musk put in $100 million of the roughly $450 million raised privately.

distractors.text: NASA, through later CRS contracts
distractors.why: CRS paid for deliveries afterward. Development was roughly split between NASA and private money.

concepts.statement: Constellation ran over cost and behind schedule and was canceled under Obama in 2010. Lori Garver argued that handing routine work to companies would free NASA for more consequential work. Obama framed the new approach as buying space transportation as a service rather than owning the vehicles.
concepts.passage: By buying the services of space transportation—rather than the vehicles themselves—we can continue to ensure rigorous safety standards are met.

questions.prompt: How did Lori Garver argue that commercialization would benefit NASA itself?
questions.answer: Companies take routine work; NASA does harder things
questions.why: She argued NASA should stop competing with the private sector by doing the same thing over and over, and invest in work of greater relevance to taxpayers, like climate research, which got under 10% of its budget.

distractors.text: Commercial vehicles would turn out safer than NASA's
distractors.why: The promise was that rigorous safety standards would still be met, not exceeded.

distractors.text: Competition would push down Constellation's costs
distractors.why: Garver wanted Constellation canceled, not competed.

distractors.text: NASA could shrink into a regulator of private launch
distractors.why: She wanted NASA investing in consequential research, not reduced to oversight.

questions.prompt: In his 2010 speech, what did Obama describe as the core of the new approach?
questions.answer: Buy transportation as a service, not the vehicles
questions.why: 'By buying the services of space transportation, rather than the vehicles themselves', companies would compete and innovate faster while NASA kept safety standards rigorous.

distractors.text: Return to the Moon on a new heavy rocket
distractors.why: That was Constellation, which his administration canceled.

distractors.text: Let companies set their own safety standards
distractors.why: He said rigorous safety standards would still be met.

distractors.text: Back one commercial champion to replace the shuttle
distractors.why: NASA deliberately kept multiple providers.

concepts.statement: COTS cost NASA about $850 million, half the cost of a single shuttle launch, and produced two new orbital rockets and cargo vehicles (SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Dragon, Orbital's Antares and Cygnus). It led to Commercial Resupply Services contracts, kept two providers as a hedge, and seeded Commercial Crew.
concepts.passage: At a cost to NASA of $850 million—half the cost of a single shuttle launch—the agency had helped develop two new orbital rockets and cargo vehicles.

questions.prompt: What did NASA get for the roughly $850 million it spent on COTS, about half the cost of one shuttle launch?
questions.answer: Two new orbital rockets and two cargo vehicles
questions.why: SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Dragon, and Orbital's Antares and Cygnus. NASA then bought routine deliveries separately, under CRS.

distractors.text: Twenty cargo deliveries to the ISS
distractors.why: That's CRS: twelve SpaceX flights and eight Orbital, bought separately for about $3.5 billion.

distractors.text: A rocket able to carry astronauts to the ISS
distractors.why: Crew came later, under Commercial Crew, with the first flight in 2020.

distractors.text: One working rocket; Orbital's was never finished
distractors.why: Both succeeded. Orbital's Antares launched Cygnus to the ISS in 2013.

concepts.statement: COTS counted as an 'inflection point' because SpaceX began launching commercial satellites on the rockets developed under NASA contract. The benefit extended beyond the ISS, and NASA really was one customer among many.
concepts.passage: SpaceX was beginning to launch commercial satellites with the rockets developed under contract with NASA.

questions.prompt: Beyond delivering cargo to the ISS, what made COTS an 'unqualified success' in the authors' telling?
questions.answer: Its rockets went on to sell commercial launches
questions.why: Once SpaceX sold launches to commercial customers, NASA was truly one customer among many. NASA's money had created an industry capability, not just a supplier. That's why the authors call it an inflection point.

distractors.text: It finished ahead of schedule
distractors.why: It took seven years, longer than first hoped.

distractors.text: It ended US dependence on Russia's Soyuz for crew
distractors.why: That came in 2020, with Commercial Crew. COTS was cargo only.

distractors.text: Its boosters were later reused
distractors.why: SpaceX first re-flew a booster in 2017. Reuse was built on COTS, but it isn't the measure the authors use.

concepts.statement: Reusable rockets became real in late 2015. Blue Origin's suborbital New Shepard crossed the Kármán line (100 km) and landed vertically in November. SpaceX landed a Falcon 9 first stage after an orbital launch in December and first re-flew a used booster in 2017.
concepts.passage: SpaceX had successfully launched a (partially) reusable orbital rocket, a feat only matched by the space shuttles.

questions.prompt: Blue Origin and SpaceX each landed a rocket in late 2015. What made SpaceX's the harder feat?
questions.answer: It came back from an orbital launch
questions.why: New Shepard went straight up past 100 km and came back down. Falcon 9's first stage landed after sending its upper stage and satellites on to orbit, a far harder problem.

distractors.text: Its booster landed on a drone ship at sea
distractors.why: Falcon 9's first stage flew back to land on the Florida coast.

distractors.text: The same booster flew again within weeks
distractors.why: Reversed. Blue Origin re-flew its booster five times in the next year; SpaceX didn't re-fly one until 2017.

distractors.text: It was carrying a crew capsule to the ISS
distractors.why: Neither carried crew. Falcon 9 was carrying communications satellites.

questions.prompt: What is the Kármán line?
questions.answer: The standard boundary of space, 100 km up
questions.why: Crossing it is far easier than reaching orbit, which takes enormous horizontal speed. That's the gap between New Shepard's feat and Falcon 9's.

distractors.text: The altitude at which orbit becomes possible
distractors.why: Orbit depends on speed, not just altitude. Suborbital New Shepard crossed the line without orbiting.

distractors.text: The upper edge of low Earth orbit
distractors.why: Low Earth orbit sits well above the line; the ISS orbits around 400 km.

distractors.text: Where Earth's gravity stops dominating
distractors.why: Gravity at 100 km is nearly as strong as at the surface.

concepts.statement: Falcon 9 launches cost about $62 million, roughly $2,800 per kilogram, less than 5% of the shuttle's cost per kilogram (though the shuttle had far more capabilities). The drop triggered new satellite companies, new launch competitors and a surge of venture capital.
concepts.passage: A mere $62 million per launch, or roughly $2,800 per kilogram. That's less than 5 percent of what it cost the shuttle (which, not coincidentally, was designed with far more capabilities).

questions.prompt: How did Falcon 9's launch cost per kilogram compare with the shuttle's?
questions.answer: Under 5% of the shuttle's
questions.why: About $2,800 per kilogram against about $60,000, roughly twenty times cheaper, at about $62 million a launch.

distractors.text: About a quarter of the shuttle's
distractors.why: Far too high. The drop was about twentyfold.

distractors.text: About half of the shuttle's
distractors.why: Far too high. The drop was about twentyfold.

distractors.text: About 0.1% of the shuttle's
distractors.why: Too low. That would be about $60 per kilogram.

questions.prompt: When comparing Falcon 9's cost with the shuttle's, what caveat do the authors add?
questions.answer: The shuttle had far more capabilities
questions.why: It had a cargo bay for satellite repair, an airlock, a robotic arm, and it carried crew. The authors say the cost gap is 'not coincidentally' related.

distractors.text: Falcon 9 is only partially reusable
distractors.why: True, and the authors note it, but it isn't the caveat on the cost comparison.

distractors.text: The shuttle figure is in 2008 dollars
distractors.why: The authors adjust for that (nearly $90,000 today), which makes the gap bigger, not smaller.

distractors.text: Falcon 9 had flown too few times to judge
distractors.why: It was flying routinely, and reusing boosters from 2017.

questions.prompt: Which of these does the chapter NOT list as a result of Falcon 9's lower launch costs?
questions.answer: Governments cutting their own space budgets
questions.why: The chapter lists more satellite companies, new launch competitors and a surge of venture capital. Cheaper launch expanded the market.

distractors.text: More satellite companies forming
distractors.why: Listed: with lower costs and more launch availability, more satellite companies emerged.

distractors.text: New launch companies challenging SpaceX
distractors.why: Listed: other launch companies formed to challenge the new leader.

distractors.text: Venture capital pouring in
distractors.why: Listed: venture capital firms poured in funding at unprecedented scale.

concepts.statement: In 2020 SpaceX carried two NASA astronauts to the ISS under the Commercial Crew program, closing the space access gap and making the commercial approach the default.
concepts.passage: Funded by the Commercial Crew program, SpaceX had defied the skeptics and closed the space access gap.

questions.prompt: Which event closed the 'space access gap' that opened when the shuttle retired?
questions.answer: SpaceX flying NASA astronauts to the ISS in 2020
questions.why: The gap was about crew. Astronauts rode Soyuz until the 2020 Commercial Crew flight.

distractors.text: A Dragon capsule docking with the ISS in 2012
distractors.why: That restored US cargo access, fulfilling COTS. Crew still rode Soyuz.

distractors.text: The first Falcon 9 booster landing in 2015
distractors.why: A milestone for reusability, not for crew access.

distractors.text: The first Falcon 9 launch in 2010
distractors.why: The rocket's debut. It carried neither cargo to the ISS nor crew.

concepts.statement: The chapter's economic frame is the First Fundamental Theorem of Welfare Economics: markets are efficient when certain conditions hold. Public goods violate those conditions, which justified central control. Over time, central control's weaknesses made even public goods costly to pursue, and space ambitions shifted to activities where the conditions come closer to holding, so markets became the better tool. NASA kept the public-goods work.
concepts.passage: as our ambitions for space grew, we sought objectives for which the "certain conditions" of the 1FTWE come closer to holding; that is, for which markets would be more efficient

questions.prompt: The authors give two reasons the shift from central control to markets made sense. Which pair?
questions.answer: Central control got costly; goals got market-friendly
questions.why: Missing prices, blunt incentives and slowing innovation made even public goods expensive to pursue. And as ambitions grew, they included activities where the theorem's 'certain conditions' come closer to holding.

distractors.text: The Soviet threat ended; NASA's budget shrank
distractors.why: Both happened, but they're context. The authors' argument is about where markets are efficient.

distractors.text: Shuttle disasters; public loss of interest in space
distractors.why: These forced the issue, but the authors justify the shift on economic grounds.

distractors.text: Rocket tech matured; private capital became available
distractors.why: Venture capital poured in after launch costs fell. In the chapter it's a result, not the reason.

questions.prompt: According to the closing section, what did COTS-style policies leave NASA free to concentrate on?
questions.answer: Exploration, prestige, cooperation, basic research
questions.why: The division of labor is the point: markets for what markets do well, NASA as central actor for goals 'less suited to private actors'.

distractors.text: Regulating the safety of commercial launch providers
distractors.why: Not what the authors list. They describe NASA's strengths as pursuing public goods.

distractors.text: Designing rockets for companies to operate
distractors.why: That's close to the old model that COTS replaced.

distractors.text: Running its own fleet for routine ISS transport
distractors.why: That's exactly what it handed to companies.

questions.prompt: By the chapter's framework, which condition would most justify keeping a space activity under central government control?
questions.answer: Everyone benefits and no one can be charged for it
questions.why: That's the definition of a public good, where the theorem's conditions fail and a market would underprovide.

distractors.text: It needs large up-front capital
distractors.why: SpaceX raised over $450 million privately during COTS. Markets can fund capital-heavy work.

distractors.text: It carries a high risk of technical failure
distractors.why: SpaceX blew up rockets at an alarming rate and still delivered under a fixed-price contract.

distractors.text: No private company has attempted it before
distractors.why: No company had built an ISS cargo vehicle before COTS either.

concepts.statement: COTS and its follow-ons worked through four mechanisms: competition between private actors, prices reintroduced via fixed-price contracts, incentives for responsible risk-taking, and letting efficient companies keep the rewards.
concepts.passage: Carefully crafted policies like COTS and its follow-ons introduced competition between private actors, reintroduced prices through fixed-price contracts, incentivized responsible risk-taking, and allowed innovative and efficient companies to reap the rewards.

questions.prompt: Central control suffered from missing price signals. Which COTS feature addressed that weakness most directly?
questions.answer: Fixed-price contracts
questions.why: The authors say COTS 'reintroduced prices through fixed-price contracts'. A set fee for a service is a price, and it reveals who can deliver for less.

distractors.text: Insight in place of oversight
distractors.why: That followed from fixed prices, but it's about NASA's working relationship, not prices.

distractors.text: Companies keeping their intellectual property
distractors.why: That made NASA one customer among many. It addresses the market's breadth, not prices.

distractors.text: Use of Space Act Agreements
distractors.why: The legal vehicle that made the changes possible, not the mechanism itself.

questions.prompt: A space agency wants cheaper lunar cargo delivery. Which design is closest to the COTS model?
questions.answer: Several firms, fixed milestone fees, firms own landers
questions.why: COTS combined competition, fixed-price milestone payments and company ownership.

distractors.text: Best firm picked, all costs reimbursed, design supervised
distractors.why: That's cost-plus with oversight, the FAR model.

distractors.text: Agency designs the lander and firms bid to build it
distractors.why: That's the traditional model: government sets the requirements, contractors implement.

distractors.text: One national champion, guaranteed all missions
distractors.why: That's the shuttle's monopoly pattern.
